chapter_title: Configuration Management with AWS Systems Manager (SSM)
chapter_summary:
Managing a fleet of servers, whether in the cloud or on-premises, can quickly become complex. Ensuring consistent configurations, applying patches, executing commands, and maintaining security can be daunting. AWS Systems Manager (SSM) is a powerful, unified management service that helps you gain operational visibility and control over your AWS resources and on-premises servers. It simplifies resource and application management, shortens the time to detect and resolve operational problems, and allows you to operate at scale. SSM is a collection of capabilities, each designed to address a specific operational challenge, all accessible from a single console.

At the heart of SSM's functionality is the **SSM Agent**. This agent must be installed and running on any EC2 instance or on-premises server that you want to manage with Systems Manager. Most Amazon Linux AMIs come with the SSM Agent pre-installed. For other operating systems or custom AMIs, you'll need to install it manually. The agent communicates with the SSM service, allowing it to receive commands, apply configurations, and send back status and output. For an instance to be managed by SSM, it also needs an IAM instance profile with the `AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore` policy attached, granting it the necessary permissions to communicate with the SSM service. A common mistake is forgetting this IAM role, which prevents instances from appearing as "managed instances" in SSM.

One of the most frequently used capabilities of SSM is **Run Command**. This allows you to remotely and securely execute commands on one or more managed instances. You can run shell scripts, PowerShell commands, or use pre-defined SSM documents (e.g., `AWS-RunShellScript`, `AWS-InstallApplication`). Run Command is perfect for ad-hoc tasks like installing software, restarting services, or collecting diagnostic information. It provides detailed output for each command execution, making it easy to verify success or troubleshoot failures. The commands are executed without needing to SSH into the instances, enhancing security by reducing the need to open inbound SSH ports.

For maintaining a desired state across your instances, **SSM State Manager** is your go-to. State Manager allows you to define and apply configurations to your managed instances at a specified schedule. This ensures that your instances are always in a compliant state, whether it's installing specific software packages, configuring services, or joining a domain. You create an association in State Manager, linking an SSM document (e.g., `AWS-ApplyAnsiblePlaybooks`, `AWS-ConfigureWindowsUpdate`) with your target instances and a schedule. State Manager then automatically applies the configuration, reporting compliance status. This is invaluable for preventing configuration drift and enforcing security baselines.

**SSM Parameter Store** provides secure, hierarchical storage for configuration data management and secret management. You can store data such as database connection strings, API keys, passwords, and license codes. Parameters can be stored as plain text (`String`), encrypted text (`SecureString` using KMS), or a list of strings (`StringList`). SecureString parameters are particularly useful for sensitive information, as they are encrypted at rest and in transit. Applications and scripts can then retrieve these parameters programmatically, eliminating the need to hardcode sensitive information in your code or configuration files. This significantly improves security and simplifies configuration updates.

Finally, **SSM Session Manager** offers a secure and auditable way to access your EC2 instances or on-premises servers without needing to open inbound ports, manage SSH keys, or use bastion hosts. Session Manager provides a browser-based shell or CLI access to your instances. All sessions are logged to CloudWatch Logs and S3, providing a comprehensive audit trail of who accessed what, when, and what commands were run. This greatly enhances security and compliance, especially for organizations with strict auditing requirements. To use Session Manager, ensure your instances have the SSM Agent installed and the correct IAM instance profile with `AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore` policy.

In summary, AWS Systems Manager is a comprehensive suite of tools that brings robust operational capabilities to your AWS and hybrid environments. By leveraging its various features, SysOps administrators can automate routine tasks, enforce configuration consistency, secure sensitive data, and provide secure access to instances, all while maintaining a detailed audit trail.

narration.text: In this lesson you will explore AWS Systems Manager, a suite of capabilities that helps you manage fleets of servers consistently and securely. You’ll learn what the SSM Agent does, why an IAM instance profile is required, and how Run Command, State Manager, Parameter Store, and Session Manager solve specific operational problems. We’ll ground each capability with a practical example: using Run Command to install a web server, storing connection strings in Parameter Store with encryption, and starting an auditable shell with Session Manager. You will also see common operational mistakes, like missing the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore role, and how SSM’s central console and logging improve visibility and compliance. By the end, you should be able to explain how SSM reduces the need for SSH, enforces desired state, and stores secrets safely—so you can automate routine work, prevent drift, and keep an audit trail for troubleshooting and compliance. Ready to dive into the components and a hands-on flow that mirrors real SysOps tasks?

screens.title: What is AWS Systems Manager (SSM)?
screens.subtitle: A unified set of capabilities for operational visibility and control

narration.text: AWS Systems Manager is a collection of capabilities designed to simplify operational management across AWS and hybrid environments. At its core, SSM centralizes tasks like running commands, enforcing configuration, storing parameters, and opening auditable sessions. The essential claim is that SSM gives you a single control plane to manage many instances consistently, reducing the need for direct SSH access and manual intervention. For example, instead of logging into each server, you can use Run Command to install software across hundreds of instances and capture output for auditing. A common misconception is that SSM replaces IAM or monitoring tools; it doesn’t. SSM integrates with IAM for permissions and with CloudWatch and S3 for logs. Another mistaken belief is that the agent alone is sufficient—SSM requires both the SSM Agent on instances and the correct IAM instance profile to allow secure communication. In practice, SSM shines when teams want repeatable, auditable operations: use State Manager to define a desired state for packages or configuration and Parameter Store to avoid hardcoded secrets. As you work through the lab steps, ask: how does centralizing these capabilities reduce risk and improve your incident response?

keyIdea.title: SSM centralizes and automates operations
keyIdea.text: Treat SSM as the unified control plane for remote commands, configuration enforcement, secret storage, and secure sessions for managed instances.

screens.title: SSM Agent and IAM instance profile
screens.subtitle: How managed instances communicate with Systems Manager

narration.text: The SSM Agent is the piece of software that must run on any server you want Systems Manager to manage. Its role is simple: establish an outbound connection to the SSM service, receive commands or configuration instructions, execute them, and return status and output. However, the agent alone is not enough. A managed instance also needs an IAM instance profile with the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy attached. That policy grants the instance permissions to call SSM APIs, write logs, and decrypt parameters when needed. A frequent operational mistake is installing the agent but forgetting the role, which results in an instance that appears unmanaged. A practical verification step is to look in Fleet Manager; managed instances appear there with a status. For a concrete example, Amazon Linux AMIs often ship with the agent preinstalled; for other OS images you must install it manually and attach the instance role. Remember: agent equals capability, role equals permission. If either is missing, SSM operations will fail. To check: confirm the SSM Agent is running locally and that the instance role includes AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore. SSM Agent and IAM instance profile means both the ssm agent and the amazonssmmanagedinstancecore iam profile are required for an instance to register and accept commands from systems manager.. In practical terms, how managed instances communicate with systems manager. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Using Run Command to execute tasks
screens.subtitle: Run shell scripts remotely and capture output for auditing

narration.text: Run Command lets you execute scripts or commands on one or more managed instances without SSH. It uses SSM documents — either AWS-provided types like AWS-RunShellScript or custom documents — to describe a command set. When you run a document, SSM schedules the work, the agent receives it, executes commands locally, and returns status and output. For example, a common ad-hoc task is installing a web server. In the lab you'll run a small shell script to update packages, install httpd, enable and start the service, and write an index page. Run Command provides per-instance output so you can confirm success or diagnose failure. A misconception is that Run Command requires inbound ports; it doesn’t. The agent makes outbound calls so no SSH port is needed. Always consider output destination: you can send command output to CloudWatch or S3 for long-term auditing. When designing operations, treat Run Command as the secure replacement for one-off SSH operations. Using Run Command to execute tasks means use run command with ssm documents to securely run scripts on many instances and capture their output for troubleshooting and auditability.. In practical terms, run shell scripts remotely and capture output for auditing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Run Command
Run Command flow
SSM document → Run Command → agent executes → output returned
Why use it
  • Execute ad-hoc maintenance without opening inbound ports.
  • Get per-instance output for verification and troubleshooting.
  • Integrate with State Manager for scheduled, repeatable runs.
Key Takeaway

Run Command is the secure alternative to manual SSH for remote operations and inspection.

Example script
This script is suitable for AWS-RunShellScript targets on Amazon Linux 2.
sudo yum update -y
sudo yum install -y httpd
sudo systemctl start httpd
sudo systemctl enable httpd
echo "<h1>Hello from SSM Run Command!</h1>" | sudo tee /var/www/html/index.html
Output options: view per-instance output in the Run Command console or send to CloudWatch/S3 for persistent logs.
Misconception
Run Command does not require inbound network access to instances because the agent initiates outbound communication with the SSM service.

screens.title: State Manager for desired state enforcement
screens.subtitle: Define associations to keep instances compliant on a schedule

narration.text: State Manager is designed to maintain a desired configuration across your fleet. You create an association that links an SSM document with target instances and a schedule. The document could apply a package baseline, configure Windows Update settings, or run an Ansible playbook. When the association runs, State Manager calls Run Command under the hood to execute the document and then reports compliance. This pattern solves configuration drift by continuously reapplying a known good state. A concrete example is scheduling a monthly patch baseline run with the AWS-RunPatchBaseline document targeting instances with a specific tag or Auto Scaling group. A common misconception is that State Manager is only for initial setup; it’s meant to run regularly to prevent drift. When designing associations, think about idempotence: documents should be safe to run multiple times without causing unintended changes. Also plan for reporting: use the compliance results so you can detect instances that fail to apply the desired state and investigate those outliers. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: SSM Parameter Store — types and use cases
screens.subtitle: String, StringList, and SecureString for configuration and secrets

narration.text: Parameter Store is a hierarchical storage for configuration values and secrets. It supports three types: String for plain text, StringList for ordered lists, and SecureString for encrypted values that use KMS. Use String for non-sensitive configuration such as region names or feature flags. Use StringList when an application needs an ordered list of values. Use SecureString when storing credentials, A P I keys, or connection strings; these are encrypted at rest and in transit. A helpful concrete example is storing a database connection string as a SecureString; your application or script can retrieve it at runtime with decryption rather than embedding secrets in source code. A common mistake is storing secrets as plain Strings; that exposes sensitive data if IAM permissions are misconfigured. When using SecureString, ensure the instance role or caller has KMS decrypt permission. Also, Parameter Store supports hierarchical naming; use a structured path like /my-app/prod/db to organize parameters. Finally, Parameter Store integrates with SSM Agent and applications via A P I calls so you can centralize configuration management in a secure way. SSM Parameter Store — types and use cases means choose string for simple values, stringlist for ordered lists, and securestring with kms for any sensitive configuration you must protect.. In practical terms, string, stringlist, and securestring for configuration and secrets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Use SecureString for secrets

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Parameter Store
Parameter types
String · StringList · SecureString
String
Plain configuration values that are not sensitive.
StringList
Comma-separated lists that your application expects in order.
SecureString
Encrypted values using KMS; used for secrets like DB credentials.
Key Takeaway

Always use SecureString for sensitive data and control KMS permissions carefully.

Concrete example
Create /my-app/db-connection-string as a SecureString with your account’s KMS key. An application using the instance role with decrypt permission can call the SSM API to fetch the decrypted value at runtime.
CLI retrieval example
aws ssm get-parameter --name /my-app/db-connection-string --with-decryption
Note: Ensure callers have KMS decrypt permission for SecureString retrieval.

screens.title: Session Manager for secure, auditable access
screens.subtitle: Access instances without SSH keys or open inbound ports

narration.text: Session Manager provides secure interactive shell access to managed instances using the SSM Agent and IAM for authentication. It avoids opening inbound SSH or RDP ports and eliminates the operational burden of distributing SSH keys. Sessions can be launched from the console or CLI and are auditable: all commands and output can be logged to CloudWatch Logs or S3, producing an audit trail of who connected and what was run. This is particularly useful for environments with strict compliance requirements. A common misconception is that Session Manager is a replacement for all remote debugging; while powerful, it is best used for command-line troubleshooting and short-lived sessions. For persistent or highly interactive GUI work, other tools may be needed. To use Session Manager, ensure the instance has the SSM Agent and the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore role. Also confirm necessary CloudWatch or S3 logging is configured if you require full session capture. Consider Session Manager the secure, auditable alternative to bastion hosts and SSH keys. Session Manager for secure, auditable access means session manager opens a secure shell without inbound network exposure and logs sessions for compliance and troubleshooting.. In practical terms, access instances without ssh keys or open inbound ports. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Parameter Store: create and retrieve a SecureString
screens.subtitle: Store a database connection string and fetch it with AWS CLI

narration.text: This guided activity shows how to place a sensitive configuration value in Parameter Store and retrieve it securely. First, open Systems Manager Parameter Store and create a parameter with a clear hierarchical name, for example /my-app/db-connection-string. Choose SecureString as the type and select the KMS key source. Paste your database connection string as the value and create the parameter. Next, verify retrieval using the AWS CLI on a host that has an IAM role with SSM and KMS decrypt permissions. Use the get-parameter command with the with-decryption option to see the decrypted value. A typical mistake is missing KMS decrypt permission on the caller, which results in an access error even if SSM read permissions exist. Also avoid storing secrets as plain Strings. After the retrieval, delete the parameter as part of clean up in the lab or rotate it if it’s intended for long-term use. This pattern keeps secrets out of code and centralizes access control and auditability for configuration values. Parameter Store: create and retrieve a SecureString means create securestring parameters with kms, retrieve them with with-decryption, and ensure callers have kms decrypt permissions.. In practical terms, store a database connection string and fetch it with aws cli. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Parameter Store Lab
Create a SecureString
Use a hierarchical name and choose KMS encryption.
  1. Open Systems Manager → Parameter Store → Create parameter.
  2. Name: /my-app/db-connection-string; Type: SecureString.
  3. Choose KMS key source and enter the connection string value.
  4. Click Create parameter and note the name for retrieval.
Remember: plan for rotation and least-privilege access to decrypted values.
Retrieve with AWS CLI
aws ssm get-parameter --name /my-app/db-connection-string --with-decryption
Common error
If you see an access denied error, check that the caller's role has KMS decrypt permissions for the key used by SecureString.

screens.title: SSM logging and audit architecture
screens.subtitle: How Run Command and Session Manager integrate with CloudWatch and S3

narration.text: SSM integrates with CloudWatch Logs and S3 to provide persistent logs and audit trails. When you run commands or start sessions, you can configure output to be sent to CloudWatch or an S3 bucket. This provides two benefits: first, you preserve output for investigation and compliance; second, you can centralize logs from many instances in one place for searching and alerting. For example, configure Run Command to deliver output to an S3 path for long-term retention while also streaming to CloudWatch for near-real-time inspection. Session Manager sessions can be recorded in the same way, capturing the commands executed and their responses. A common misconception is that SSM automatically archives everything; you must enable and configure the desired output destinations and ensure the S3 bucket and CloudWatch log groups have appropriate access permissions. Consider lifecycle policies and encryption for stored logs. Architecting SSM logging thoughtfully ensures you have both fast troubleshooting data and durable compliance records. narration.text: Operational problems often arise from a few recurring mistakes when using Systems Manager. First, forgetting to attach the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore role means the agent cannot register—installing the agent without the role leaves an instance unmanaged. Second, storing secrets as plain Strings exposes sensitive data in the event of misconfigured IAM—use SecureString with KMS and restrict decrypt permissions. Third, neglecting to configure Run Command or Session Manager output destinations means you lose auditability; enable CloudWatch or S3 logging and set retention. Fourth, design SSM documents to be idempotent so scheduled State Manager runs don't produce side effects. For debugging, inspect per-instance Run Command output and Fleet Manager for connectivity and agent health. Also, when operating at scale, tag resources and use resource groups or Auto Scaling group targeting to keep associations manageable. These practices reduce friction, prevent configuration drift, and ensure that your automated operations are both secure and traceable.
